title: What do common consulting and business terms mean, in plain English?
description: The business terms you will meet in case interviews, from ARPU to utilisation, each explained simply with an example.
hook: Case interviews come with their own vocabulary, and it can make you feel like an outsider. It shouldn't. Here are the terms you are most likely to meet, each explained in plain English with an example.
body:
ARPU

Average revenue per user: revenue in a period divided by the number of customers.

Example: $514M a year ÷ 12.6M subscribers ÷ 12 ≈ $3.40 a month.

ARR

Annual recurring revenue: the yearly value of all active subscriptions. Used for software and other subscription businesses.

Example: 2,000 customers paying $15,000 a year = $30M ARR.

Breakeven

The point (in units sold, or time) where revenue covers all costs, so profit is exactly zero.

Example: $12M launch cost ÷ $0.80 contribution per bar = 15M bars to break even.

CAC

Customer acquisition cost: sales and marketing spend divided by the number of new customers it brings in.

Example: $900k of ads ÷ 10,000 new customers = $90 each.

CAGR

Compound annual growth rate: the steady yearly growth that takes you from a start value to an end value.

Example: Doubling in 7 years ≈ 10.4% a year.

Cannibalisation

When a new product or channel takes sales from your own existing ones instead of winning new customers.

Example: If 60% of delivery orders replace a café visit, most delivery sales aren’t really new.

Capex and opex

Capex is spending on assets that last for years, such as a plant or equipment, paid upfront and used over their life. Opex is the ongoing cost of running the business (staff, rent).

Example: A $150M plant is capex; its yearly running cost is opex.

Churn

The share of customers who leave in a period.

Example: 2% monthly churn means the average customer stays about 50 months.

Contribution margin

Price minus the variable cost of one unit: what each sale contributes towards fixed costs and profit.

Example: $1.50 price − $0.70 variable cost = $0.80 per bar.

Cost of capital

The return investors expect for the risk they take. A project only creates value if it returns more than this.

Example: A project returning 8% destroys value if the cost of capital is 10%.

DCF

Discounted cash flow: valuing a business or project by adding up its future cash flows, each reduced (discounted) to what it is worth today.

Example: $100 received in a year is worth about $91 today at a 10% discount rate.

Due diligence

The checks a buyer does before an acquisition or investment.

Example: Testing whether a recycling company can really make the food-grade plastic it promises.

Earn-out

Part of an acquisition price paid later, only if the business hits agreed targets.

Example: $160M upfront plus up to $20M if premium contracts are signed.

EBITDA

Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation: a rough measure of operating cash profit, used to value companies.

Example: A gym chain makes $25M EBITDA.

Enterprise value (EV)

What the whole business is worth to all its funders: equity value plus net debt (debt minus cash).

Example: Equity $245M + net debt $60M = EV $305M.

Fixed and variable costs

Fixed costs don’t change with volume (rent). Variable costs rise with each unit made or sold (ingredients).

Example: App commissions are variable; head-office salaries are fixed.

Hypothesis

Your best guess at the answer, stated early so you can test it with data.

Example: "I suspect delivery costs are the issue, so I’d start there."

IRR

Internal rate of return: the yearly return an investment earns over its life. Private equity funds often target about 20%.

Example: Tripling your money in 6 years ≈ 20% a year.

LTV

Lifetime value: the profit a customer brings over the whole time they stay. Compare it with CAC.

Example: $12 a month × 80% margin × 19 months ≈ $182.

Margin vs markup

Margin is profit as a share of price. Markup is profit as a share of cost.

Example: Cost $80, price $100: margin 20%, markup 25%.

MECE

Mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive: buckets that don’t overlap and together cover everything important.

Example: Revenue and costs are MECE for profit.

Money multiple

Cash a fund gets back divided by cash it put in. Also called MOIC.

Example: $40M in, $130M out ≈ 3.25× the money.

Multiple

A quick way to value a business: a number times its profit or revenue, based on what similar companies sell for.

Example: 8× EBITDA of $25M = $200M.

Net revenue retention

What last year’s customers are worth this year, after cancellations, downgrades and upgrades, as a share of what they were worth before.

Example: $30M of customers now worth $27M = 90%.

NPV

Net present value: the value today of all future cash flows, minus the upfront cost. Positive NPV means the investment pays.

Example: −$1.5M upfront + $153k a year for 25 years at 8% ≈ +$133k.

Operating leverage

How much profit swings when sales change. A business with mostly fixed costs has high operating leverage: a small rise in sales lifts profit a lot, and a small fall hurts a lot.

Example: An airline with 80% fixed costs sees profit jump when planes fill up.

Opportunity cost

The value of the best alternative you give up by choosing something.

Example: A factory line making housings can’t also make brackets worth $2.8M a year.

Payback period

How long it takes for an investment to earn back what it cost.

Example: $20M upgrade earning $10M a year pays back in 2 years.

Perpetuity

The value today of a steady cash flow that goes on forever: cash flow ÷ discount rate.

Example: $5M a year at 8% is worth $62.5M.

Pricing power

The ability to raise prices without losing many customers, usually from a strong brand, a unique product or little competition.

Example: A software tool that firms rely on daily can raise prices 5% a year.

Private label

A retailer’s own-brand products, usually cheaper than branded ones.

Example: A supermarket’s own cornflakes.

Switching costs

The money, time or hassle a customer faces to move to a rival. High switching costs make customers stay.

Example: Moving a bank’s core systems to a new vendor takes two years.

Synergies

Extra value created by combining two businesses: cost savings or extra revenue neither could get alone.

Example: Shared logistics saving $5M a year.

Utilisation

How much of available capacity is actually being used.

Example: 460M litres made in a 500M-litre plant = 92% utilisation.
outro: Read it once, then try it on a practice case today while it is fresh. One real attempt teaches more than three re-reads. The glossary also lives on the glossary page, where you can search it.
